title: Electromagnetic Waves
short_intro: Electromagnetic waves are coupled oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagating through space, transferring energy and momentum. They are transverse waves generated by accelerated charges and travel through free space with a constant speed equal to the speed of light.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic characteristics of electromagnetic waves, transverse nature, electromagnetic spectrum order, wavelength/frequency ranges, and the relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes (E = cB).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Maxwell's equations, displacement current, derivation of the wave equation for electric and magnetic fields from Maxwell's equations, Poynting vector, energy density, momentum, and radiation pressure.

prerequisites: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral forms
Vector calculus (curl, divergence, and vector identities)
Alternating current fundamentals and displacement current concept

concept_notes.heading: Nature and Generation of Electromagnetic Waves
bullets: Electromagnetic waves are produced by accelerated or oscillating charges, which create time-varying electric fields that in turn induce time-varying magnetic fields.
The electric field vector (E), magnetic field vector (B), and the direction of propagation (k) are mutually perpendicular, forming a right-handed triad (E × B points along k).
They are transverse in nature and do not require any material medium for propagation, travelling through a vacuum with speed c = 1 / sqrt(μ<sub>0</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Maxwell's Equations and Displacement Current
bullets: Maxwell modified Ampere's circuital law by introducing the displacement current density J<sub>d</sub> = ε<sub>0</sub> (∂E / ∂t) to maintain consistency with the equation of continuity.
Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction ensures that a changing magnetic field produces an electric field (curl E = -∂B / ∂t).
The generalized Ampere-Maxwell law states that magnetic fields can be generated by both conduction currents and changing electric fields.

concept_notes.heading: Energy, Momentum, and Poynting Vector
bullets: The energy density associated with an electromagnetic wave is shared equally between the electric field component (&frac{1}{2}ε<sub>0</sub>E<sup>2</sup>) and the magnetic field component (&frac{1}{2μ<sub>0</sub>}B<sup>2</sup>).
The rate of energy transport per unit area is given by the Poynting vector S = &frac{1}{mu<sub>0</sub>} (E × B).
Electromagnetic waves exert radiation pressure on surfaces they strike, transferring linear momentum p = U / c when completely absorbed.

concept_notes.heading: Electromagnetic Spectrum
bullets: The electromagnetic spectrum spans a continuous range of frequencies and wavelengths, categorized from radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, to gamma rays.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed c in free space, but differ significantly in their methods of generation and interaction with matter.
High-frequency waves (X-rays, gamma rays) exhibit more particle-like interactions, whereas low-frequency waves (radio, microwaves) exhibit pronounced wave characteristics.

derivations.title: Relation between Electric and Magnetic Field Amplitudes
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum along z-axis
steps: Let the electric field be E = E_{0} \sin(kz - \omega t)\hat{i} and magnetic field be B = B_{0} \sin(kz - \omega t)\hat{j}
Apply Faraday's law \nabla \times E = -\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} in Cartesian coordinates
Evaluate the curl of E: \frac{\partial E_{x}}{\partial z} \hat{j} = k E_{0} \cos(kz - \omega t)\hat{j}
Evaluate the time derivative of B: -\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} = \omega B_{0} \cos(kz - \omega t)\hat{j}
Equate the components: k E_{0} = \omega B_{0}, which simplifies using \frac{\omega}{k} = c

graphs_and_experiments.title: Orthogonal Sinusoidal Oscillations of E and B Fields
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A coordinate system with z-axis as propagation direction, showing an electric field oscillating along the y-axis (sine wave) and a magnetic field oscillating along the x-axis (cosine wave in phase with E).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the transverse nature and spatial-temporal quadrature relationship of the coupled fields.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT to identify field orientations and polarization directions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Chart
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A logarithmic scale spanning from 10<sup>-18</sup> m to 10<sup>4</sup> m, marking regions of gamma rays, X-rays, UV, visible, IR, microwaves, and radio waves with increasing wavelength.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the inverse relation between frequency and wavelength across the spectrum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct factual questions on ordering of frequencies, wavelengths, and detection methods.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hertz's Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An induction coil connected to spark gap transmitter spheres, paired with a distant wire loop acting as a receiver spark gap.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proved the existence of electromagnetic waves by observing induced sparks across the receiver gap via resonance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually for historical context and verification of Maxwell's theory.

solved_numericals.question: The amplitude of the magnetic field part of a harmonic electromagnetic wave in vacuum is B_{0} = 510 nT. What is the amplitude of the electric field part of the wave?
solution_steps: Identify given values: B_{0} = 510 \times 10^{-9} T, c = 3 \times 10^{8} m/s.
Use the relation between electric and magnetic field amplitudes: E_{0} = c B_{0}.

solved_numericals.question: Light with an energy flux of 18 W/cm^{2} falls on a non-reflecting surface at normal incidence. If the surface has an area of 20 cm^{2}, find the average total momentum delivered to the surface during a 30-minute time span.
solution_steps: Convert intensity to SI units: I = 18 W/cm^{2} = 18 \times 10^{4} W/m^{2} = 1.8 \times 10^{5} W/m^{2}.
Calculate total energy incident: U = I \times A \times t where A = 20 \times 10^{-4} m^{2} and t = 30 \times 60 = 1800 s.
For complete absorption, momentum p = U / c = \frac{6.48 \times 10^{5}}{3 \times 10^{8}}.
Calculate final momentum: p = 2.16 \times 10^{-3} kg \cdot m/s.

solved_numericals.question: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric field oscillates sinusoidally at a frequency of 2.0 × 10^{10} Hz and an amplitude of 48 V/m. Calculate the average energy density of the electromagnetic wave.
solution_steps: Identify given values: E_{0} = 48 V/m, \varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12} C^{2}/N \cdot m^{2}.
Recall the formula for average energy density: u_{avg} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_{0} E_{0}^{2}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Plane wave approximation assumes wavefronts are infinite flat planes, valid only locally far from small localized sources.
Linear medium assumptions apply; nonlinear optical effects at extremely high laser intensities are neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Electromagnetic waves require a material medium like ether or air to propagate.
common_misconceptions.correct: Electromagnetic waves are self-propagating oscillations of electric and magnetic fields and can travel through a perfect vacuum.
common_misconceptions.why: Unlike mechanical waves (sound, water waves), EM waves do not rely on mechanical vibrations of matter.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave carries much less energy than the electric field.
common_misconceptions.correct: The electric and magnetic fields carry equal amounts of average energy density in free space.
common_misconceptions.why: Since E<sub>0</sub> = cB<sub>0</sub> and u<sub>E</sub> = &frac{1}{2}ε<sub>0</sub>E<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> while u<sub>B</sub> = B<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> / (2μ<sub>0</sub>), substituting c<sup>2</sup> = 1/(μ<sub>0</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>) shows u<sub>E</sub> = u<sub>B</sub>.

quick_revision: EM waves are transverse waves with E and B fields mutually perpendicular and normal to the direction of wave propagation.
Field Amplitude Ratio: E_{0} = c B_{0}
